opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what each of them thinks language fundamentally *is*. Chomsky's picture, at least in its classic form, is that there's this innate, specialized faculty, a universal grammar, some kind of hardwired module, and that recursion in particular is the crown jewel that makes human language what it is. And the corollary, which he's been quite vocal about, is that statistical learning from exposure can't get you there. The famous poverty of the stimulus argument: kids don't hear enough data to learn grammar, so it must be built in.

Dan Everett's work, especially with the Pirahã in the Amazon, pushes on that from a very different direction. His view is that language is a cultural tool. It's shaped by the needs, the social life, the cognition of a community, and it's learned and invented using fairly general-purpose cognitive capacities rather than a dedicated language organ. Whether or not you accept every claim he makes about Pirahã lacking recursion, and that's been fiercely debated, the deeper point is that languages vary far more than a strong universal grammar would predict, and that the variation tracks culture.

Now, the reason this matters so much to me is that we've basically run the experiment. Large language models are, in a sense, the most extreme possible test of the poverty of the stimulus argument. They start with no grammar built in at all, just a very general sequence-learning architecture, and through exposure to language they acquire grammar, recursion, long-range dependencies, all of it, extraordinarily well. You can argue they see more data than a child, and that's a fair point, but it does demolish the in-principle claim that you *can't* learn this statistically. And the efficiency gap is narrowing too.

So for me, Everett's framing just fits better with what we now see. Language looks less like a crystalline formal system sitting in a special box in the brain and more like something learned, social, predictive, and grounded in the general capacity to model sequences and other minds. Chomsky also tends to dismiss the idea that these models tell us anything about language or cognition, and I think that's a mistake. They're telling us a lot, maybe not everything, but a lot, and much of it is pointing in Everett's direction.

r001.rationale: The response links Everett’s Pirahã work and the debated claim that Pirahã lacks recursion to a challenge to Chomsky’s view that recursion is central to language.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes Chomsky’s theoretical claims and his dismissal of language models, but does not say that his work neglects empirical study of actual languages.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I like and respect both of them, and I've had the chance to talk with both of them. But the thing that draws me to Dan's view is that it's fundamentally an empirical and evolutionary account, and Chomsky's, at least in its strong form, isn't.

Chomsky's position, as I understand it, is that there's a universal grammar, a language organ, something that arrived more or less all at once, maybe via a single mutation, and that recursion, the ability to embed phrases within phrases, is the defining feature of human language. And crucially, in that view, language isn't really about communication. It's a kind of internal cognitive faculty that happens to get externalized.

Dan spent years living with the Pirahã in the Amazon, and what he came back with was a language that, as far as he could tell, doesn't use recursion in the way the theory requires. Now, you can argue about the details of that, and people have. But to me the bigger point is methodological. Dan starts from language as a cultural technology, a tool that evolved gradually because it was useful for people living together, coordinating, telling stories, keeping track of social relationships. It's shaped by culture and environment, and it co-evolved with our brains over a very long time, probably starting with Homo erectus, long before anatomically modern humans. That's a story that's continuous with everything else we know about evolution. Things don't usually appear fully formed.

And honestly, the thing that really clinched it for me was watching large language models learn. These systems have no innate universal grammar. They have a very generic architecture and a lot of data, and they acquire syntax, including recursion, just by predicting what comes next in a social, communicative stream of text. If grammar required a dedicated innate module, that shouldn't work. The fact that it does work is, to me, pretty strong evidence that the structure of language is something that emerges from learning in a rich environment, which is much closer to Dan's picture than to Noam's. Chomsky has dismissed language models as irrelevant to understanding language, and I think that's exactly backwards. They're the first real experiment we've been able to run on this question.

r001.rationale: It says Pirahã appears not to use recursion “in the way the theory requires,” presenting it as a challenge to Chomsky’s proposed requirement.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Chomsky’s strong-form account with an empirical, evolutionary approach, but does not clearly say Chomsky neglects empirical study of actual languages.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling about Everett’s approach is that it treats language as something we do together—a cultural practice that develops in response to the need to communicate. That puts social interaction, history, and meaning at the center of the picture.

Chomsky’s approach emphasizes the underlying formal structure and the possibility of an innate, language-specific grammar. There’s clearly something biological that makes language possible, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the grammar itself has to be built in. It could emerge from more general capacities for learning, cooperation, and understanding other people’s intentions, interacting with cultural evolution.

Everett’s work on Pirahã makes that difference concrete, although the interpretation of his findings is contested. I wouldn’t say one language settles the whole argument. What I prefer is the direction of explanation: start with people communicating in a particular social world, and ask how linguistic structure emerges from that.

r001.rationale: It says Everett’s work on Pirahã illustrates the difference, but does not present Pirahã as a counterexample to Chomsky’s proposed requirements for language.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Chomsky’s emphasis on formal structure with Everett’s social and cultural focus, but does not criticize Chomsky for neglecting empirical study of actual languages.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling about Everett’s approach is that it treats language as something people do together, embedded in culture and social life. The question becomes: how do communities develop and transmit these extraordinarily powerful tools for coordinating, sharing knowledge, and thinking?

Chomsky’s approach puts much more emphasis on an innate, specifically linguistic structure. There’s obviously something innate about our capacity to learn language—we’re biological organisms—but that doesn’t establish that the structure of grammar itself has to be specified in advance.

Everett gives learning, culture, and communicative need a much larger explanatory role. I find that a more productive starting point. It also makes linguistic diversity central to the investigation: differences between languages are evidence about what language can become under different circumstances.

That doesn’t mean every claim Everett makes is right, or that Chomsky’s contributions weren’t profound. It’s a preference for an explanatory direction: understanding language through its development and use, in brains and between people.
